sn4.1:1.4: “Grueling work” (_dukkarakārikā_) refers to the self-mortification he practiced for six years before awakening ([mn12:56.1](), [mn100:27.5]()), which was similar to Jain practices ([mn14:17.5]()).
sn4.1:1.6: I follow the MS reading here. Sinhalese editions have “steady, mindful” instead of “freed”. Commentary is silent.
sn4.1:5.2: The split compound _amaraṁ tapaṁ_ also occurs at  [thag3.1:1.4](), and at [snp2.2:11.4]() we have _amarā bahū tapā_. The commentary explains that _amara_ here is “immortality”, and the phrase means “fervent mortification aimed at immortality”. However, I find this unconvincing, one reason being that _amara_ is an adjective (and thus must be glossed with an abstract noun in dative, _amarabhāvatthāya_). It is simpler to assume Pali has an idiomatic sense of _amara_ as “endless”, which occurs here, in the phrase _amarāvikkhepa_ ([dn1:2.23.1]()), and in the Niddesa’s _amarāvitakka_ ([cnd12:6.1]()). Then _amarā_ and _bahū_ are synonyms. I cannot find any use in Sanskrit that parallels this, but _amara_ is noted by Edgerton in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit as “a high number”.
